questions.question: Gram-Schmidt takes vectors $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_k$ in a real inner product space, sets $\boldsymbol{v}_j=\boldsymbol{a}_j-\sum_{i<j}\frac{\boldsymbol{a}_j\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_i}{\boldsymbol{v}_i\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_i}\boldsymbol{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_j=\boldsymbol{v}_j/\|\boldsymbol{v}_j\|$. Why must the inputs be linearly independent?
options: It guarantees every $\boldsymbol{v}_j\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, so dividing by $\|\boldsymbol{v}_j\|$ is allowed
It is what makes the computed vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ orthogonal to one another
It makes every $\boldsymbol{a}_j\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_i$ nonzero, so each step changes $\boldsymbol{a}_j$
It makes the output the same for every ordering of the input vectors

questions.question: Gram-Schmidt with the dot product runs on linearly independent $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{a}_2,\boldsymbol{a}_3$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$; $\boldsymbol{v}_1=\boldsymbol{a}_1$ and the orthogonal vector $\boldsymbol{v}_2$ have been computed. Which formula gives $\boldsymbol{v}_3$?

Gram-Schmidt turns linearly independent $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_k$ into orthonormal $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k$ with $\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_j\}=\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_j\}$ for every $j$. Which relation between outputs and inputs follows for every $j$?
options: $\boldsymbol{q}_j$ is orthogonal to its own input $\boldsymbol{a}_j$
$\boldsymbol{q}_j$ is orthogonal to each later input $\boldsymbol{a}_i$, $i>j$

questions.question: In Gram-Schmidt on linearly independent $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_k$ in a real inner product space, with $\boldsymbol{v}_j=\boldsymbol{a}_j-\sum_{i<j}\frac{\boldsymbol{a}_j\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_i}{\boldsymbol{v}_i\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_i}\boldsymbol{v}_i$, which description of $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ is correct?
options: The component of $\boldsymbol{a}_j$ orthogonal to the single vector $\boldsymbol{a}_{j-1}$
What is left of $\boldsymbol{a}_j$ after removing its projection onto the later inputs

questions.question: A student runs Gram-Schmidt on linearly independent $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_k$, computes the orthogonal vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_j$, but skips the final step $\boldsymbol{q}_j=\boldsymbol{v}_j/\|\boldsymbol{v}_j\|$. Which property of the output is lost compared with $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k$?
options: Orthogonality, which only the scaled vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_j$ have
Independence, so that some later $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ could become $\boldsymbol{0}$
Only unit length; orthogonality and the nested spans remain

questions.question: Apply Gram-Schmidt with the dot product to $\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,1)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}_2=(1,3)^{\top}$. What is $\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{a}_2-\frac{\boldsymbol{a}_2\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_1}{\boldsymbol{v}_1\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_1}\boldsymbol{v}_1$, with $\boldsymbol{v}_1=\boldsymbol{a}_1$?
Gram-Schmidt with the dot product starts from $\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,2,2)^{\top}$, so $\boldsymbol{v}_1=\boldsymbol{a}_1$. What is the first orthonormal output $\boldsymbol{q}_1$?

Take $\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,2,0)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}_2=(-2,1,5)^{\top}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the dot product. What does the second Gram-Schmidt step $\boldsymbol{a}_2-\frac{\boldsymbol{a}_2\cdot\boldsymbol{a}_1}{\boldsymbol{a}_1\cdot\boldsymbol{a}_1}\boldsymbol{a}_1$ return as $\boldsymbol{v}_2$?

Gram-Schmidt with the dot product is run on $\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,0,1)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{a}_2=(2,1,2)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{a}_3=(0,1,0)^{\top}$, no two of which are parallel. Which of the computed vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_3$ is zero?
options: None, since no input is a multiple of another input
Only $\boldsymbol{v}_2$, since $\boldsymbol{a}_2=2\boldsymbol{a}_1+\boldsymbol{a}_3$ depends on the others
Both $\boldsymbol{v}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_3$, as all three inputs are involved

questions.question: In the $\boldsymbol{q}$-form of Gram-Schmidt, $\boldsymbol{v}_j=\boldsymbol{a}_j-\sum_{i<j}(\boldsymbol{a}_j\cdot\boldsymbol{q}_i)\boldsymbol{q}_i$. With the dot product on $\mathbb{R}^2$, $\boldsymbol{q}_1=(0.6,0.8)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}_2=(1,0)^{\top}$. What is $\boldsymbol{v}_2$?

Classical Gram-Schmidt computes every coefficient $\boldsymbol{a}_j\cdot\boldsymbol{q}_i$ from the original $\boldsymbol{a}_j$; the modified version subtracts the projections one at a time from the updated vector. Which comparison of the two versions is correct?
options: They give different orthonormal bases even in exact arithmetic, as the coefficients differ
The classical one is more accurate in floating point, since it updates the vector less often
They agree in exact arithmetic; the modified one keeps orthogonality better in floating point
The modified one needs no division by $\|\boldsymbol{v}_j\|$, since its vectors keep unit length

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^4$ with the dot product, $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2$ are orthonormal and $\boldsymbol{e}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{e}_4$ is the standard basis. How can Gram-Schmidt, discarding any zero $\boldsymbol{v}_j$, extend $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2$ to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^4$?
options: Run it on $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2,\boldsymbol{e}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{e}_4$; $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2$ come out unchanged
Run it on $\boldsymbol{e}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{e}_4$ only; the outputs are then orthogonal to $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2$
Run it on $\boldsymbol{e}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{e}_4,\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2$; the input order has no effect
Run it on $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2,\boldsymbol{e}_1,\boldsymbol{e}_2$; any two added vectors suffice

questions.question: Gram-Schmidt with the dot product turns linearly independent $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_k$ into orthogonal $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k$, where $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ is $\boldsymbol{a}_j$ minus its projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_{j-1}\}$. How do $\|\boldsymbol{v}_j\|$ and $\|\boldsymbol{a}_j\|$ compare?
options: $\|\boldsymbol{v}_j\|\geq\|\boldsymbol{a}_j\|$, with equality only in the first step $j=1$
$\|\boldsymbol{v}_j\|=\|\boldsymbol{a}_j\|$, since the removed part is orthogonal to $\boldsymbol{v}_j$
Either norm can be the larger one, depending on how the inputs $\boldsymbol{a}_i$ are ordered

questions.question: Gram-Schmidt with the dot product is applied to $\boldsymbol{a}_1=(3,4)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}_2=(1,7)^{\top}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, giving $\boldsymbol{q}_1=\tfrac{1}{5}(3,4)^{\top}$. What is the second output $\boldsymbol{q}_2$?

Gram-Schmidt with the dot product has produced the orthogonal vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,0,1)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(1,0,-1)^{\top}$ from $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{a}_2$. The next input is $\boldsymbol{a}_3=(1,2,3)^{\top}$. What is $\boldsymbol{v}_3$?

On $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the dot product let $\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,0)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}_2=(1,1)^{\top}$. In the order $(\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{a}_2)$, Gram-Schmidt gives $\boldsymbol{q}_1=(1,0)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{q}_2=(0,1)^{\top}$. What is the second output $\boldsymbol{q}_2$ when the inputs are processed in the order $(\boldsymbol{a}_2,\boldsymbol{a}_1)$?

Gram-Schmidt with the dot product turns linearly independent $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{a}_2,\boldsymbol{a}_3$ into $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2,\boldsymbol{q}_3$. It is then run on $\boldsymbol{b}_1=\boldsymbol{a}_1$, $\boldsymbol{b}_2=\boldsymbol{a}_2+5\boldsymbol{a}_1$, $\boldsymbol{b}_3=\boldsymbol{a}_3-2\boldsymbol{a}_2$. What are the new outputs?
options: Different vectors, since $\boldsymbol{b}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{b}_3$ differ from $\boldsymbol{a}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{a}_3$
The same vectors up to sign, since only the nested spans are preserved
The same $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2$, but a different third vector $\boldsymbol{q}_3$
Exactly $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\boldsymbol{q}_2,\boldsymbol{q}_3$ again, with no sign changes

questions.question: Gram-Schmidt turns linearly independent $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_k$ into orthonormal $\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k$. Another orthonormal list $\boldsymbol{u}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{u}_k$ satisfies $\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{u}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{u}_j\}=\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_j\}$ for every $j$. What must hold?
options: Each $\boldsymbol{u}_j=\boldsymbol{q}_j$: the nested spans fix every sign too
Each $\boldsymbol{u}_j=\pm\boldsymbol{q}_j$: the list is unique up to signs
No link to $\boldsymbol{q}_j$: $\boldsymbol{u}_j$ may be any unit vector of the $j$-th span
Each $\boldsymbol{u}_j=\pm\boldsymbol{q}_j$, but only if the $\boldsymbol{a}_j$ are orthogonal

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}^2$ use the inner product $\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}M\boldsymbol{y}=x_1y_1+2x_2y_2$ with $M=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$. Gram-Schmidt with this inner product is applied to $\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,1)^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}_2=(1,0)^{\top}$. What is $\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{a}_2-\frac{\boldsymbol{a}_2^{\top}M\boldsymbol{a}_1}{\boldsymbol{a}_1^{\top}M\boldsymbol{a}_1}\boldsymbol{a}_1$?

Gram-Schmidt with the dot product, discarding any zero $\boldsymbol{v}_j$, is run on $\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,2,2)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{a}_2=(2,4,4)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{a}_3=(1,0,0)^{\top}$. Which orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{a}_2,\boldsymbol{a}_3\}$ results?
options: $\tfrac{1}{3}(1,2,2)^{\top}$ alone, as the run stops at $\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{0}$
